extracted.intended_audience: school, college, and university administrators, Title IX coordinators, legal counsel, and stakeholders responding to Title IX rulemaking
extracted.subtask_short: defining sexual harassment under Title IX
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply the Department's regulatory standards and interpretive guidance for what constitutes sexual harassment under §106.30 and related Title IX provisions, and how recipients must respond. Includes prongs of the definition, standards of proof/assessment, and procedural obligations for recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.30 three‑pronged definition of sexual harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibiting conduct on the basis of sex that is either quid pro quo harassment, unwelcome conduct so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive that it effectively denies a person equal access to education, or sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, or stalking under the Clery Act and VAWA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department believes this formulation better captures prohibited conduct under Title IX and makes clear that Clery/VAWA offenses are included. The definition is intended to identify conduct that constitutes sex discrimination by denying equal access to education; it is not a 'zero tolerance' ban of all unwelcome or uncomfortable conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quid pro quo harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: quid pro quo harassment (as one prong of §106.30)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counts as sexual harassment under §106.30 and is a standalone category that does not require satisfaction of the Davis elements (severe, pervasive, objectively offensive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Davis standard: severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive
rubrics_metrics.description: Unwelcome conduct on the basis of sex that is so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive that it effectively denies a person equal access to education (the Second prong, derived from Davis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department adopts the Davis framework for unwelcome conduct that is not quid pro quo or a Clery/VAWA offense. The standard is a fact‑based inquiry, intended to avoid imposing Title IX liability for every offensive remark while ensuring responses to behavior that rises to denial of equal access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clery Act/VAWA offenses included as standalone types
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual assault (including rape), dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking under the Clery Act and VAWA are included in §106.30 as types of sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These offenses are treated as sexual harassment without requiring demonstration of severity, pervasiveness, objective offensiveness, or denial of equal access, because denial of equal access is assumed for these offenses. The Department uses the FBI UCR definitions to broadly define sexual assault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Davis elements determined under a reasonable person standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The elements in the Davis definition (severe, pervasive, objectively offensive, and denial of equal access) are determined under a reasonable person standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations revise §106.30 to specify that whether conduct meets Davis elements must be judged by whether a reasonable person (standing in the complainant's shoes) would find it so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive. This responds to comments urging an objective-reasonableness requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on recipients to evaluate reports; not on complainant to 'prove' elements
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no magic language required from complainants; the burden of describing or proving elements of §106.30 does not fall on complainants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must evaluate reports in a common sense manner, taking into account factors such as a complainant's age, disability status, and other circumstances that affect how the complainant communicates or experiences the conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator impartiality requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX Coordinators are specifically required under the final regulations to serve impartially, without bias for or against complainants or respondents generally or for or against an individual complainant or respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This impartiality requirement is aimed at reducing arbitrary or biased determinations and incentivizes careful, thoughtful, and reasonable evaluation of each report or formal complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may address non‑Title IX misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Dismissal for Title IX purposes does not preclude action under another provision of the recipient's code of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If conduct does not meet §106.30, recipients may still investigate or discipline under state law, institutional policies, or their own codes of conduct. Recipients also may elect to use the §106.45 grievance process for non‑Title IX misconduct if they choose, or use disciplinary procedures that do not comply with §106.45.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must post Title IX Coordinator contact information (§106.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact information for the Title IX Coordinator, including an office address, telephone number, and email address, must be posted on the recipient's website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This posting requirement is intended to simplify reporting (for example, for community college students with limited physical-campus connections) by making a clear reporting channel available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable person perspective in evaluating severity/pervasiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Severity, pervasiveness, and objective offensiveness must be determined from the perspective of a reasonable person standing in the shoes of the complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation is fact‑dependent and should take into account ages and developmental abilities of involved parties, disability, power differentials, prior trauma, and other context-specific factors that affect how conduct is experienced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance with free speech and academic freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The Davis formulation is intended to safeguard free speech and academic freedom while requiring response to verbal conduct so serious that it loses First Amendment protection and denies equal access to education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severity and pervasiveness are required elements in part to avoid chilling speech and to avoid imposing liability for every offensive remark in an academic setting; recipients may still address non‑Title IX conduct through other policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of sexual assault uses FBI UCR and does not require physical force
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of sexual assault referenced in §106.30 broadly includes all forcible and nonforcible sex offenses described in the FBI's Uniform Crime Reporting system; these offenses turn on lack of consent rather than an element of physical force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department believes this broad definition reflects the range of sexually violative experiences that traumatize victims, and includes perpetration by acquaintances, dates, or intimate partners (not just strangers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients violate regulations if response is clearly unreasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient that responds to a report of sexual harassment in a manner that is clearly unreasonable in light of the known circumstances violates the final regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision creates an enforcement incentive for Title IX offices to carefully and reasonably evaluate reports, preventing arbitrary or dismissive handling of complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform definition across educational settings with common‑sense application
rubrics_metrics.description: The §106.30 definition applies equally in elementary, secondary, and postsecondary contexts, but may be applied in a common‑sense manner that takes into account ages and developmental abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department rejects tailoring the definition by educational level, preferring a uniform statutory definition applied with nuance to account for developmental differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Severe' and 'pervasive' are separate but interacting inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department views severity and pervasiveness as separate elements (not automatically conflated), although course-of-conduct context may make conduct qualify as both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argued for 'severe OR pervasive' or conflation; the Department maintains the separate inquiries while acknowledging that pervasive conduct can render an otherwise less severe act actionable in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions may publish lists of per se harassment situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final regulations prevents a recipient from publishing a list of situations that the recipient has found to meet §106.30, or from creating a list of situations that violate the recipient's own code of conduct even if they do not violate Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department notes such lists could promote consistent application of the harassment definition within a campus community and advise potential victims and perpetrators about conduct found to violate Title IX or institutional policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent and related definitions left to recipients
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department leaves flexibility to recipients to define consent and terms commonly used to describe absence or negation of consent (e.g., incapacity, coercion, threat of force).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice recognizes varying State laws requiring particular consent definitions and allows recipients to adopt definitions reflecting local legal requirements and community values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of Supreme Court framework (Gebser and Davis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department relies on the Supreme Court's Gebser and Davis opinions as appropriate principles to guide interpretation and enforcement of Title IX in the non‑sex discrimination context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department treats Title IX as prohibiting sex discrimination when harassment is so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive that it effectively denies equal access to education, in line with those precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarification that Title IX is not a catch‑all for all uncomfortable conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX does not require recipients to respond to every act of conduct that 'makes me feel uncomfortable'; only conduct that meets the statutory/principled thresholds triggers mandatory Title IX responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients retain discretion to encourage reporting of any unwanted conduct and to address conduct outside Title IX under non‑Title IX policies; the Department believes this approach avoids chilling speech while protecting equal access where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision to §106.45(b)(3)(i): dismissal does not preclude other action
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations revise §106.45(b)(3)(i) to clearly state that dismissal for Title IX purposes does not preclude action under another provision of the recipient's code of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change clarifies confusion from the NPRM and makes explicit that recipients obliged by state law or institutional policy to investigate broader misconduct may do so even when the conduct is not Title IX sexual harassment.
